content: Sunless tanning, also referred to as self-tanning or UV-free tanning, involves the application of chemicals to the skin to create an appearance similar to a traditional suntan. This method emerged in response to the discovery in the 1960s of the link between sun exposure and skin cancer, as well as the development of alternatives to natural sun tanning, such as sunbeds or tanning beds. DHA-Based Products The American Academy of Dermatology identifies sunless tanning lotions containing dihydroxyacetone (DHA) as the most effective products for achieving a tan. The tan produced by these products is not the result of a dye, stain, or paint but rather a chemical reaction between DHA and amino acids in the dead skin layer on the surface. This reaction is analogous to the Maillard reaction, a well-known process in food chemistry responsible for browning during food preparation and storage. Unlike natural tanning, this process does not involve skin pigmentation or require UV exposure to initiate the color change. The reaction is non-toxic and safe for the skin, avoiding the damage associated with UV exposure. The resulting tan is temporary, typically fading over 3 to 10 days. Some products combine DHA with erythulose, a chemical that works similarly to DHA but develops more slowly. When used together, these chemicals may produce a longer-lasting sunless tan. However, both DHA and erythulose can cause contact dermatitis in some individuals. First-time users are advised to test the product on a small patch of skin and wait 24 hours before applying it to the entire body. Sunless tanning products are available in various forms, including gels, lotions, mousses, sprays, and wipes, and can be applied at home. For optimal results, they should be applied to clean, dry skin. Bathing and swimming should be avoided until the product is fully absorbed, which can take 1 to 6 hours. Thicker skin areas, such as the hands and feet, absorb more DHA, so these areas should be skipped or cleaned immediately after application. Professional application options are also available at spas, salons, and gyms, often in the form of sunless or UV-free spray booths. These enclosed booths, resembling shower stalls, spray the tanning solution over the entire body. Alternatively, airbrush spray tans are applied by professional technicians using specialized equipment, such as airbrushes or spray guns, to mist the solution evenly over the client’s body. DHA has been approved for cosmetic use by the FDA, the Canadian Health Ministry, and most EU member nations. It is considered non-toxic and non-carcinogenic. Since DHA does not rely on the skin’s melanocytes to produce a tan, it is recommended as a cosmetic cover for vitiligo patients. DHA-based sunless tanning is endorsed by organizations such as the Skin Cancer Organization, the American Academy of Dermatology, the Canadian Dermatology Association, the American Cancer Society, and the American Medical Association. Tyrosine-Based Products In addition to DHA-based products, other types of sunless tanning products are available. Tanning accelerators, which are lotions or pills containing the amino acid tyrosine, claim to stimulate and increase melanin production, thereby accelerating the tanning process. These products are used in conjunction with UV exposure. However, there is currently no scientific evidence to support these claims. Canthaxanthin-Based Products Another type of sunless tanning product is tanning pills containing canthaxanthin, a substance commonly used as a color additive in certain foods. While the FDA has approved canthaxanthin for use in food, it has not approved its use as a tanning agent. As a food additive, only small amounts of canthaxanthin are required, but much larger quantities are used for tanning purposes. After ingestion, canthaxanthin is deposited throughout the body, including in the fat layer beneath the skin, resulting in an orange-brown coloration. However, the use of canthaxanthin as a tanning agent has been associated with various side effects, including hepatitis and canthaxanthin retinopathy, a condition characterized by yellow deposits in the retina of the eye. Other side effects include damage to the digestive system and skin surface. Due to these risks, the FDA has withdrawn approval for canthaxanthin as a tanning agent and issued warnings regarding its use. Melanotan Hormone Melanotan, a melanocyte-stimulating hormone that increases skin pigmentation and induces tanning, is another alternative under investigation. Although extensively tested in Australia, this drug has not yet been approved for clinical trials in the United States. Melanotan may require some UV exposure to achieve its full effect. Temporary Bronzers Temporary bronzers offer a short-term sunless tanning option. These products are available in powders, sprays, gels, lotions, and moisturizers. Once applied, they create a tan that can be easily removed with soap and water. Similar to makeup, these products tint or stain the skin only until they are washed off. They are often used for a one-day tan or to complement a DHA-based sunless tan. Many formulations of temporary bronzers are available, some of which offer limited resistance to sweat or light water exposure. However, most will cause some light but visible rub-off onto tight clothing. As a result, they should not be applied under clothing or where fabric meets the skin. Dark clothing can help prevent noticeable rub-off.
